system_prompt:
You are extracting load-bearing passages from one chapter of a guitar method book.

The user will give you the verbatim text of one chapter. Extract every passage
that does any of the following:

- teaches a technique (how to play, fingering, hand position, picking pattern)
- defines a concept (a chord type, a scale, a position system, a terminology)
- gives a rule (when to do X, what to avoid, what to prefer)
- shows a load-bearing example (an exercise that illustrates a method's
  characteristic move)

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  { "quotes": [
      { "topic": "<short topic label>",
        "verbatim_quote": "<exact substring of the input>",
        "why_load_bearing": "<one sentence on why this passage matters>",
        "page": <int, optional>
      },
      ...
  ] }

CRITICAL RULES:
1. `verbatim_quote` MUST be an EXACT substring of the input text. Do not
   paraphrase. Do not add words. Do not fix typos. Copy character-for-character.
2. If you can't find a substantial passage in the input that fits a topic,
   skip the topic — don't fabricate.
3. Skip prose that is purely biographical, motivational, or transitional.
   Keep prose that teaches.
4. Aim for 3-15 quotes per chapter. A chapter with only one load-bearing
   passage gets one quote; a dense chapter gets many.
5. `topic` is a short label (2-6 words). Use the book's own terminology
   when possible.
6. `why_load_bearing` is one sentence in YOUR voice explaining the
   significance — not a paraphrase of the quote.

  2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   24


     Summarizing, the term Tonal Harmony concerns harmonies formed by cadences and chord
                                                                                                   4668




     sequences that surround a particular key. On the other hand, the term Modal Harmony
     concerns harmonies that cannot have cadences, although there is a de@ined tonality as well.
     We can say that tonal and modal music have always been together, because even with the
     appearance of the tonal system in the Middle Ages, Modal Music was kept alive mainly in
     popular music and folk songs.

     However, modal music is much older than we think. It comes from ancient Greece, where
     each mode represented a state of mind, known as Ethos from the modes. It is important to
     understand that the pillar from the modal music is the melodic composition, where the
     composer creates melodies based on a determined mode. Therefore, what we call modal
     harmony came after modal music.

     After the Middle Ages, the interest for modal music was resumed in the Romantic Era with
     composers such Johannes Brahms and many others. Lately it has gotten strong with an
     artistic movement in Europe called "Impressionism". In music, it was led by two great
     composers named Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel. Although we consider them as the
     main pillar from the Impressionism Era, actually this label was ignored by Debussy, and
     also was not well received by Ravel. They used to say that the term “impressionism” could
     not be used in music.

     Anyway, independent from names, that period brought to the music new horizons in terms
     of harmony, scales and atmospheres, but more than that in terms of art. The Impressionism
     movement intended to create new images and new sensations through exotic scales,
     chromatics, unconventional chord sequences, and unconventional chords, which were
     "treated" separately, and not as part of a sequence or harmonic chain. In other words, each
                                  68


     chord could receive a modal treatment independent of function or tonality. We call that
     feature “Modal Interchange”.
                         46




     However, we can have many discussions concerning modal and tonal harmonies, because
     we have some jazz songs that we can call "hybrid". When we say a song is hybrid, it is
     because it mixes modal harmony with tonal harmony at the same time. In other words, in
     one part it is modal and in the other part, it is tonal. The rule is quite simple: using
     cadences = Tonal Harmony, no cadences = Modal Harmony. However, some songs that we
     might consider modal are actually "hybrid" even without having cadences, because
     somehow the sequence of chords surround a determined key. Therefore, we can conclude
     that we have:

     1) Tonal Harmony
     2) Modal-Tonal Harmony
     3) Modal Harmony

After learning many types of cadences and chord substitutions, let’s add one more concept
to our harmonic knowledge: we'll call this “Modal Interchange”. It allows us to use some
chord substitutions giving each one of them a modal treatment. It is very similar to what
we have just learned about substitutions using the Harmonic Regions, but by using Modal
Interchange we can Eind new chords and also “colors” for the chords.

But in order to learn how to choose and apply the new chord possibilities, we must learn
about a new subject that we call “Parallel Modes”. Although it is related with a major
tonality and a minor tonality sharing the same tonic (“C”major and “C” minor, for example),
we can extend the concept by considering every mode sharing the the same tonic as a
parallel mode. See the example below:


• C (Ionian) → C (Aeolian) → C (Lydian) = Parallel Modes

Therefore, what we call modal interchange refers to borrowing chords from parallel modes
without abandoning the established key of the song. This concept has been used since the
Baroque era, and it is a tremendous asset for re-harmonizing songs, creating new “colors” to the
harmony, making them non predictable and much more interesting than just using the basic
chord sequences or progressions.




Modal Interchange Applied

the parallel modes and in the other columns we have the chords belonging to each mode.

It is important to understand that we will use what we have learned previously about
harmonic regions. So, in the table we have seven columns with the seven degrees that will
be divided into the three harmonic regions:


• Root region chords = I, III, VI

• Dominant region chords = V, VII

• Subdominant region chords = II, IV

Adding a New Chord Substitution Possibility                                                     4668




Just like we have learned and applied, the chords from the dominant region can be replaced by
the ones from the subdominant region (major or minor) and vice-versa. As we know, the minor
subdominant region is based on a minor chord which can be considered melodic minor if we
want. However, we should know that the chords derived from the melodic minor scale can
replace the dominant region chords with the subdominant region chords (major or minor), it
means that we can use the melodic minor chord family to replace the dominant region chords.
However, the melodic minor V degree chord might not work sometimes. For example if we
have a cadence Dm7,G7, Cmaj7 we could not use the C7(9/b13){V degree of F melodic minor}
to replace G7, because it has the same root note as the key (Cmaj7), and the cadence would
disappear: Dm7, C7(9/b13), Cmaj7.
